purpose:
To approve amendments to the
social value policy.
content:
To approve amendments to the
social value policy.

The Cabinet Member for Finance &
Commissioning:
 
Approved the proposed updates to the policy,
specifically the revised table in Section 1.7, to:

·      
Reflect improved clarity around expectations for social value
delivery.

·      
Increase weighting percentages to better align with local
government best practice and support the MAT (Most Advantageous
Tender) approach.

These changes ensure Lichfield District
Council remains aligned with regional practice, maximises community
benefit, and strengthens its commitment to embedding social value
in procurement.


1.    
Option considered: Incorporating the revised weighting
guidance and commitment expectations into the broader Procurement
Strategy rather than maintaining a standalone Social Value
Policy.
Reason not pursued:
This approach was discounted as it would reduce the visibility,
influence, and strategic importance of the Council’s social
value ambitions. A standalone policy better supports clear
implementation, external communication, and alignment with the
Lichfield 2050 Strategy.
 

2.    
Option considered: Keeping the previously approved version
of Section 1.7 without amendments.
Reason not pursued: New
insights from benchmarking and training indicate that local
authorities commonly apply a 15% weighting to social value in
tenders. Updating the policy aligns with this standard, ensuring
the Council remains competitive and progressive in its
approach.

2003
 

Decisions&
Reasonsof LichfieldDistrict Council

LicensingSub
CommitteeHearing on12th August

Applicationfor
determination of objection to a
temporary

event notice under the licensing act 2003
for Wibbly
Woods
 
 

 




Councillors

Campbell-Butcher

 





Other officers in
attendance - Christine Lewis Elections and Democratic
Manager
 
 
 
 

Decision and
reason:

 

The Sub-committee sat
to hear an application for a Temporary Event Notice for a festival
known as Wibbly Woods scheduled to take place between 3 and 7
September 2026 at Fradley Woods between 16:00 and 00:00 on
Thursday, 11:00 and 04:00 Friday and Saturday, 11:00 and 00:00 on
Sunday. 

 

An objection was
received from the Environmental Health Department for the Council,
in relation to the licensing objective – the prevention of
public nuisance over concerns about noise nuisance being created by
the event.

 

The Sub-committee had
to decide whether it was appropriate to issue a counter notice
pursuant to S105(2)(b) of the Licensing Act 2003 to the premises
user.  The Sub-committee was mindful
that it was not able to impose
conditions on the Notice and its
decision was effectively a ‘yes’ or a ‘no’ to the event
taking place.

 

In making its decision
the Sub-Committee had regard to the Licensing Act 2003,
the Section 182 Statutory Guidance as
well as its own statement of licensing policy.

 

It heard from the
applicants that each year the organisers try to learn from the previous event and
make adjustments in
order to control the noise nuisance.

 

The organisers proposed that this year they would
employ an ‘acoustician’ to assist in dynamically
managing the sound levels at the festival. The applicant also
suggested that there may have been a number
of complaints received regarding previous events which were
not valid and, in any event, the number of complaints received
were very few in the context of the
total number of residents in the area.

 

The Committee heard
from the Environmental Health Officer for the Council that the
event in 2025 had received 230 noise complaints from people living
as far away as 2.85 miles from the Premises. The Committee further
heard that legal action for the 2025 event was being considered by
the Council against the applicant for carrying on the playing of
music until 02:00, despite only being permitted to do so until
23:00. The Environmental Health Officer informed the Committee that
no legal action was taken on the basis the applicant agreeing not to apply for future events within
Lichfield District. Despite this, the applicant is now making a
further application for an event within Lichfield
District.

 

The Sub-committee gave
significant weight to the Environmental Health officers concerns and noted that they are the
experts and the responsible authority in this field. The Committee
also considered that the applicant has been saying, continually,
that things will be different for the next event but –
despite this – the complaints have not only not stopped, but
have increased.

 

The Sub-committee
considered the Section 182 Guidance
particularly paragraph 7.35 relating to the scale, location and
timing of the event and concerns regarding public nuisance arising
from noise levels.

 

Accordingly the sub-committee considered that to permit the event to take place would constitute a
risk of undermining the licensing objective for the prevention of
public nuisance.  Despite the case that
the applicant put forward in support of the event, the Committee
considered it appropriate to issue a counternotice – in
essence it refuses the temporary event notice
application.

 

The parties are
reminded of their right to appeal to the magistrates court within 21 days of this
decision.

 

12:12 – Meeting
ended.

 

Right of Appeal

 

All parties are
reminded that under the provisions contained within Schedule 5 of
the Licensing Act 2003, there is the right of appeal against the decision of the Licensing
Authority to the Magistrates Court, such an appeal is to be made
within twenty-one days of the date of the notification of the
decision.

 

Dated 12th August
2026
 

 
Signed CouncillorBrian Yeates (Chair)
topline: The Lichfield District Council has decided to refuse a temporary event notice for a festival due to concerns about noise nuisance.

The Cabinet Member for Operational Services,
Parks & Waste:
 
Approved the award of the call off contract to
Contenur (UK) Limited for the supply of
140 litre, 180 litre and 240 litre wheeled bins for an initial
two-year term until 31 August 2028, with an option to extend for up
to two-years, subject to costs being within the approved budget
framework.
 
Accepted the delegation of the decision to
utilise the optional two-year extensions to the responsible Cabinet
Member, based on supplier performance and a recommendation from the
responsible director, subject to the cost being within approved
budgets.

2.1       The Lichfield District and
Tamworth Joint Waste Service provides a wheeled bin collection
service to approximately 80,000 properties across both
districts.
 
2.2       Each household is
typically issued a minimum of three bins, plus food waste caddies
which have been procured separately:
 

·      
Black for refuse

·      
Blue for dry mixed recycling (plastics, glass, cans)

·      
Brown or green for garden waste (brown in Lichfield District and
green in Tamworth Borough)

·      
Purple for card and paper (rural rounds only)
 
2.3       Sizes offered range
from 140 litre to 360 litre to accommodate household needs and
encourage waste minimisation.
 
2.4       Bins are delivered
to new households and are replaced when reported as damaged, lost
or stolen.
 
2.5       In 2024/25, a total of
6,127 bins were delivered to residents across both council areas,
reflecting consistent demand for both new and replacement bins.
 
2.6       To maintain service
standards, the Joint Waste Service must ensure that adequate stock
levels are always maintained to allow for timely deliveries and
avoid disruption to residents.
 
2.7       This procurement exercise
was conducted under a closed framework agreement, meaning that only
suppliers who had already been awarded a place on the framework
were eligible to bid. No additional suppliers outside of that
framework could submit a tender.
 
2.8       Following award of
the contract for 360 litre bins, we were made aware of cost
increases to the 140, 180 and 240 litre bins due to market factors.
Subsequently, and in line with the framework procedures, we asked
all tenderers to re-submit their costs for 140, 180 and 240 litre
bins.
 
2.9       Quality scores
remained unchanged from the original tender submissions with only
costs being re-evaluated.
 
2.10     Following evaluation in
accordance with the framework requirements, Contenur (UK) Limited achieved the highest overall
score, and the contract award is within approved budgets.
 
2.11     Contenur (UK) Limited is an established supplier of
waste and recycling containers to local authorities and other
organisations across the UK.
 
2.12     The framework also enables
engagement with suppliers within or near the West Midlands region,
supporting local economic benefit and operational efficiency.


·      
Do nothing: This would leave the Joint Waste Service without a
contract and reliant on spot buying, resulting in cost
inefficiencies, supply chain risks, and potential delays in
delivering bins to residents.
 

·      
Re-run the procurement: Repeating the procurement process would
cause unnecessary delays, risking stock depletion and operational
disruption during periods of ongoing bin demand.
topline: The Cabinet Member for Operational Services, Parks & Waste has decided to award a contract for the supply of wheeled bins for a waste collection service.

The Leader:
 
Approved the freehold acquisition of 2 bed
house in Lichfield for the sale price of £255,000, with a
further £10,000 set aside for associated legal costs and
repair/maintenance works
 
Noted that the council will work with Homes
England ongoing to determine whether any external funding is
available to contribute to the purchase and delivery of this
accommodation unit. Should funding be available, any underspend of
capital monies to fund this property will be maintained in the
capital budget for further purchases.

The acquisition will increase the
council’s supply of suitable temporary accommodation, reduce
reliance on expensive nightly-paid accommodation, improve outcomes
for vulnerable households, and support the council’s housing
and homelessness duties.
 
The purchase also represents long-term value
for money by creating a council-owned asset.

Continue using private temporary accommodation
(not recommended due to higher ongoing costs and limited
availability).
topline: The Cabinet Member Decision has decided to acquire a 2 bed house in Lichfield to increase temporary accommodation supply.

The Cabinet Member for Visitor Economy,
Ecology & Climate Change approved to enter into the S106
agreement for Oakley Spring Farm Habitat Bank at Oakley Spring
Farm, Ford Lane, Chorley, Lichfield, WS13 8BX that will include a
30-year Habitat Management and Monitoring Plan.

The Environment Act 2021 required all
development in England to provide a minimum of 10% biodiversity net
gain. Where this gain cannot be delivered on site, developers must
seek to offset this requirement off site, either through the
purchase of BUs from a registered Habitat Bank, or by purchasing
Biodiversity Credits from Natural England.
 
The Act also put a Duty on us as a Local
Planning Authority to ensure that sufficient BUs are available for
offsetting in our district (more easily allowing development to
fulfil the statutory requirement).
 
By agreeing to enter into a 30-year agreement
to monitor the delivery and condition of the proposed Oakley Spring
Farm Habitat Bank, it will allow the Bank to be listed on the
Natural England Biodiversity Gain Sites Register and begin to
officially operate as a Habitat Bank (that is, to provide
Biodiversity Units to developers to meet their Statutory
Biodiversity Net Gain requirement). This will enable more
development to take place in the district, by providing local (and
therefore more cost-effective) Biodiversity Units for local
developments.
 
The site (approx. 12 ha) comprises one arable
field and a series of pasture fields, which are intensively grazed.
The proposal is to bring the arable field into use as pasture, with
all fields subjected to a conservation grazing regime, raising rare
/ heritage breeds (such as of sheep and/or cattle).  – resulting in approximately 50 BUs being
created. By bringing back heathland on this site and into active
management for biodiversity benefit, the site will positively
contribute to both Lichfield District and UK national biodiversity
goals.

1. For amendments to be made to the S106 &
HMMP. These will then need to be conveyed and agreed by all parties
before signing and sealing can take place. 
 
2. For Lichfield District Council to not enter
into this agreement.
topline: The Cabinet Member has decided to approve a 30-year agreement for a Habitat Bank at Oakley Spring Farm to meet biodiversity net gain requirements for development in the district.

The Cabinet Member for Community and Public
Protection:
 
1.1       Reviewed and
approved the CVS prospectus for 2027-2030.
 
1.2       Approved the launch
of the programme and application process.

The community and voluntary sector represents
the very best of local communities in action. Every day, volunteers
and community organisations bring people together, support health
and wellbeing, strengthen community resilience and help residents
to thrive. The Council has a long-standing commitment to supporting
the sector and recognises it as a vital partner in delivering
services, addressing local challenges and achieving the ambitions
set out within LD2050. Through sustained investment and
collaboration, the Council aims to enable community organisations
to grow, innovate and continue making a significant difference to
residents across the district.
 
Reflecting the significant contribution that
community and voluntary organisations make to our district, the
Council has sought to increase the level of funding available
through the 2027-30 CVS Funding Programme. While £603,780 was
originally allocated within the Medium Term Financial Strategy
(MTFS), it is proposed to increase the overall funding envelope to
£1,172,367 by bringing together a number of approved budget
streams. This includes funding for localised transport initiatives,
which will support a dedicated community transport funding lot. The
increased funding represents a substantial investment in the
district's community and voluntary sector and enabling more
organisations to deliver services and projects that improve
outcomes for local residents.
 
The 2027-30 CVS Funding Programme will be
launched through the publication of a funding prospectus (Appendix
A), which sets out the programme's objectives, funding priorities,
eligibility criteria and application process. The prospectus is
intended to provide clear, transparent and accessible information
to help community and voluntary organisations to submit
applications.
 
The Council has reflected on the application
process that was used previously and has sought to streamline it as
much as possible and look to reduce the administrative burden on
community organisations. As such, a single-stage application
process will be used in this upcoming round.
 
The minimum and maximum grant awards will
remain unchanged from the last funding round, at £1,000 and
£50,000 respectively. For the community transport funding
lot, the maximum award will be £25,000.  Applicants will be asked to demonstrate a 10%
contribution towards their project. To ensure the programme remains
accessible to organisations of all sizes, this contribution can be
provided through in-kind support, such as volunteer time, donated
resources or the use of community facilities, recognising the
significant value that community organisations and volunteers
already contribute to delivering positive outcomes for local
residents.
 
The prospectus will be launched 30th July 2026
and will be open for 7 weeks.  Decisions
on awards are due to be approved by Cabinet in November 2026.

Do nothing and not launch a new Community and
Voluntary sector funding programme for 2027-30.  This would reduce support for the community and
voluntary sector and weaken the delivery of key community services
and outcomes.
topline: The Cabinet Member has decided to approve a funding programme for the Community and Voluntary sector for 2027-2030.

purpose:
To consider options for the
Trade Waste Service.
content:
To consider options for the
Trade Waste Service.
 

The Cabinet:
 
2.1 Approved the progression of a formal sale
process for the council’s trade waste service, including the
transfer of the customer base, associated contracts and operational
assets.
 
2.2 Delegated authority to the Cabinet Member
for Operational Services, in consultation with the Section 151
Officer and Director of Resident & Business Services, to
approve and complete a sale, provided the financial outcome does
not create a pressure on the Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
beyond the key decision threshold.
 
2.3 Agreed that any proposed sale which would
result in an MTFS pressure exceeding the key decision limit will be
brought back to Cabinet for a further decision.

The council operates a long-standing
discretionary trade waste service for approximately 470 local
businesses. The service provides refuse and dry recycling
collections but does not currently offer food waste
collections.
 
National Simpler Recycling reforms require all
businesses to have separate food waste collection arrangements by
31 March 2027. The council is not funded or equipped to provide a
commercial food waste service, creating a structural gap in the
current offer.
 
Customer behaviour is already changing, with
early signs of decline. This is expected to accelerate as
regulatory requirements take effect, and businesses move to
providers offering integrated waste services, specifically after 31
March 2027 when all businesses regardless of size must recycle
their food waste.
 
Maintaining the current model will result in
ongoing customer attrition, falling income and a gradual loss of
value, impacting the council’s financial position.
Conversely, a managed sale of the service would:
• Secure value while the customer base
remains viable.
• Support businesses to access compliant,
full-service waste provision.
• Avoid significant capital investment
and operational risk.
• Enable the council to exit a declining
and increasingly specialist market.
• There would be no redundancies, with
existing staff redeployed within the wider waste service.
 
This paper proposes and seeks approval to
progress with a managed sale of the service.


·      
Do nothing: Continued customer decline, falling income and loss of
value

·      
Invest in a commercial food waste service: Requires significant
capital investment, operational expansion and entry into a
competitive market with no guaranteed return

·      
Partial retention: Unlikely to be viable as businesses consolidate
services with single providers and costs of delivering a reduced
service exceed income.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the progression of a formal sale process for the council's trade waste service to address upcoming regulatory requirements and changing customer behavior.

content:
The Cabinet:
 
Delegated authority to the Cabinet Member for
Housing and Local Plan in conjunction with the Chief Executive, to
carry out the operational and administrative decisions set out in
Appendix 1.

This report seeks Cabinet approval for a
series of delegations to support preparation of the new Local Plan
under the Town and Country Planning (Local Planning) (England)
Regulations 2026. The new plan-making system requires Local Plans
to be prepared within a 30-month period and to progress through
three statutory Gateway stages. To meet these requirements, the
Council needs clear and timely arrangements for managing routine
operational, technical and administrative decisions.
 
The report recommends authority is delegated
to the Cabinet Member for Housing and the Local Plan, in
consultation with the Chief Executive, to carry out the delegations
listed in Appendix 1, to support efficient programme management and
reduce the risk of delay, particularly in meeting the Gateway 1
deadline of 31 October 2026. It does not delegate approval of the
two main statutory Local Plan consultations in June–July 2027
and May–June 2028, which will remain subject to Cabinet
approval. Strategic decisions on the content of the Local Plan,
including draft policies and site allocations, will therefore
continue to be considered through the appropriate member
decision-making process.

There is no effective alternative to
delegating key aspects of plan-making if we are to produce the
Local Plan within 30 months. Cabinet could choose not to agree one
or more recommendations in this report or could propose an
alternative delegation arrangement. In that case, a revised report
could be brought back to Cabinet on any outstanding matters.
However, this would increase the risk of not passing Gateway 1 by
31st October, which is the Government’s deadline for
authorities that have withdrawn a plan under the previous
system.
 
To not agree the recommendations, would create
uncertainty over which elements of plan-making require Cabinet
decisions. This would make it less likely that the Council could
pass Gateway 1, as streamlined project management and governance
arrangements are needed to maintain the 30-month programme.
 
Gateway 1 is a self-assessment, but the
results are shared with MHCLG. Overall, this option would be likely
to delay preparation of the Local Plan and increase the risk that
it would not be completed within 30 months. The Government also has
powers under the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act to intervene
to accelerate plan-making.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to delegate authority to the Cabinet Member for Housing and Local Plan for operational and administrative decisions in the preparation of a new Local Plan.

purpose:

content:
To note the report and the
issues raised on this.

The Cabinet:
 
2.1. Reviewed the report including the level
of general and earmarked reserves and issues raised within and note
that Leadership Team with Cabinet Members will continue to closely
monitor and manage the Medium Term Financial Strategy.
 
2.2. Approved £8,592,000 of Capital
Programme slippage related to 2025/26 being added to the Approved
Budget in 2026/27 as outlined at APPENDIX C.
 
2.3. Delegated responsibility to the Cabinet
Member for Finance and Commissioning and the Director Finance,
Environment and Community to make updates to Prudential Indicators
based on more up to date information as the accounts are finalised
in advance of approval by Council. That Cabinet, subject to review
by Audit Committee, recommends to Council:
 
2.4. Approved the actual 2025/26 Prudential
Indicators.

The Medium Term Financial Strategy originally
projected general reserves at 31 March 2026 would be
£5,803,301. General reserves were £5,263,564, a
decrease of (£539,737) related to:
• The originally projected general
reserves did not take account of the difference between the
budgeted and actual use in 2024/25 of (£56,363).
• The actual use of general reserves in
2025/26 principally to fund Cabinet priorities of (£483,374)
compared to the Original Budget of £0.
 
Leisure centres were £282,754 higher
than the Budget principally due to lower
 income. The budget performance
will need to be kept under review given the level of financial risk
related to leisure centres.
 
At the end of 2025/26, there are no
significant financial risks that need to be
 highlighted to the Council as
shareholder in relation to LWMTS financial performance.
 
The Capital Programme was (£8,511,445)
lower than the Approved Budget on the cinema development
(£3,763,000), social housing (£1,331,589) and food
waste collections (£1,281,672). It is recommended that this
budget slippage is carried forward to 2026/27 when spend is planned
to take place.
 
Income from Capital Receipts was lower than
the Approved Budget by £2,078.

These are considered as part of the ongoing
development of the Strategic Plan and the Medium Term Financial
Strategy
topline: The Cabinet has decided to note a financial report, approve capital programme slippage, and delegate responsibility for updates to Prudential Indicators.

To note the report and the
issues raised on this.

The Cabinet:
 
2.1. Reviewed the contents of this report and
the progress against planned actions in the Action Plan for
2025/26, Key Performance Indicators for 2025/26, the updated
self-assessment against the National Procurement Strategy and
progress on Procurement projects for 2025/2026.
 
2.2. Delegated authority to the relevant
Cabinet Member and Director of Finance, Environment and Community
(S151) to approve the Future Procurement Plan/Pipeline for 2026/27,
as set out in APPENDIX E. This will enable procurement exercises to
proceed, with contract awards being approved either through a
Cabinet Member Decision or Cabinet Approval, as appropriate.
 
2.3. Reviewed the update on Modern Slavery and
Human Trafficking for 2025/26.
 
2.4. Approved the suggested amendments to
KPI’s.

The Procurement Team was established in
Oct/Nov 2020 with the original Procurement Strategy being approved
in December 2020.
 
In September 2025 the second Procurement and
Commissioning Strategy was approved by Cabinet to cover 2025-2029
and builds on the solid foundations established through the
previous strategy.

procurement projects of 15.34% with improvements to the National

The redevelopment of the former Debenhams
building is a key element of the Council’s wider programme of
city centre regeneration and long-term investment in Lichfield
district.
 
Over recent years, this programme has focused
on strengthening the local economy, enhancing the quality and
accessibility of public spaces, and improving leisure and cultural
provision for residents and visitors. This has contributed to
increased usage of leisure assets and reinforced the
district’s attractiveness as a place to live, work and
visit.

and strategically important location within Lichfield city centre.
Its redevelopment, as previously approved by the Council, will
bring the building back into active use as a new leisure and
hospitality destination, including an Everyman Cinema and
complementary hospitality uses. The development is intended to
support increased footfall, strengthen the evening economy and
contribute to the ongoing vitality of the city centre.

content:
DECISION OF LICHFIELD DISTRICT COUNCIL’S
ASSESSMENT SUB-COMMITTEE
 

08 JULY 2026
 

DECISION REGARDING A COMPLAINT AGAINST DISTRICT
COUNCILLOR D. CROSS – LICHFIELD DISTRICT COUNCIL
 
Present:
 
District
Councillors: Woodward (Chair),
Ashton, Harvey-Coggins, Leung, Salter,
 
Officers: M
Hooper (Monitoring Officer), C Lewis (Deputy Monitoring Officer), W
Stevenson (Principal Governance Officer), L. Fowkes (External
Investigating Officer - Monitoring Officer at South Staffordshire
District Council)
 
Independent Person: J Jardine
 
 
Absent:
 
Subject
Member: Cllr Cross
 
Cllr Cross
had not notified any participant that he would not be attending the
hearing. The Sub-Committee delayed the commencement of the hearing
by 10 minutes to allow for late arrival. At 6:10 p.m. the
Sub-Committee resolved to proceed in the absence of the Subject
Councillor in accordance with paragraph 1(a)(i) of the Procedure
for Assessment Sub-Committees, being satisfied that there was
insufficient reason for failure to attend.
 
A further
check of the premises was undertaken at 6:20 p.m. in the event that
Cllr Cross had arrived after the commencement of the hearing. No
attendance was recorded.
 
 
Hearing
 
The hearing
took place in accordance with the District Council’s
arrangements for dealing with Member Code of Conduct
complaints.
 
The
complaint before the Assessment Sub-Committee (‘the
Sub-Committee’) related to a voicemail message left by Cllr
Cross on the 7 September 2025. During the message Councillor Cross
made statements concerning the complainant’s position as an
elected councillor and a planning application submitted by the
complainant.
 
The
Sub-Committee considered:
 

the final
Investigation Report prepared by the external investigating
officer;
the
evidence presented at the meeting
the views
of the Independent Person;

.
 
 
 
Decision
The
Sub-Committee carefully considered the Investigation Report, the
evidence presented at the hearing and the views of the Independent
Person.
The
Sub-Committee considered that although the voicemail arose against
the background of a personal disagreement, statements expressly
concerned the Complainant’s elected office and the
determination of a planning application by the Council. The
Sub-Committee therefore found that the conduct was sufficiently
connected with Councillor Cross’s role as a councillor for
the Code of Conduct to apply.
The
Sub-Committee found that the threat to have the Complainant removed
from Council was disrespectful and intimidating. It amounted to
bullying notwithstanding that Councillor Cross did not personally
possess the power to remove an elected councillor from
office.
The
Sub-Committee also found that the statement concerning the planning
application conveyed a threat that Councillor Cross would use, or
attempt to use, his position and influence as a councillor to
interfere with the Council’s planning process and
disadvantage the Complainant.
The
Sub-Committee considered that threats by an elected councillor to
remove another councillor from office and interfere with a
regulatory decision were capable of undermining public confidence
in the proper use of elected office and in the impartiality of the
Council’s decision-making arrangements. The conduct therefore
also brought the office of councillor and the Council into
disrepute.
In
reaching its decision, the Sub-Committee took account of both the
words used and the manner in which they were delivered in the
voicemail recording.
The
Sub-Committee duly found that, on the balance of probabilities,
Councillor Cross had breached the Members' Code of
Conduct.
The
Sub-Committee found that the conduct amounted to:

a failure to treat
another councillor with respect (paragraph 1.1);

 

bullying behaviour
(paragraph 2.1);

 

conduct that could
reasonably be regarded as bringing the role of councillor and the
Council into disrepute (paragraph
5.1);

 

an attempt to use the
position of councillor improperly to disadvantage another person
(paragraph 6.1).

 
Sanctions
The Sub-Committee considered the actions available
and was mindful that any sanction imposed should be reasonable,
proportionate and relevant to the subject member’s
behaviour. 
In reaching its decision the Committee noted that the
subject member had accepted making the
comments, acknowledged the findings of the investigation, offered
to undergo training and offered an apology.
Following its deliberations the Sub-Committee agreed
the following sanctions:

Censure
the subject member.

 

Recommend
that the subject member should be removed from Planning Committee
and not be appointed to Planning Committee or other
Committee/Sub-Committee exercising regulatory functions for the
remainder of the municipal year.

 

Councillor
Cross be requested to submit a written apology to the Complainant
in a form approved by the Chair of the Assessment
Sub-Committee.

 

Given the
previous breach of the code of conduct by the subject member and
failure of the Subject Member to amend his behaviour as a result of
previous training, that the Monitoring Officer be asked to identify
suitable targeted training/mentoring that deals directly with the
four areas of the code that have been breached.
topline: The Assessment Sub-Committee has decided to censure District Councillor D. Cross for breaching the Members' Code of Conduct and impose sanctions including removal from Planning Committee and targeted training/mentoring.

purpose:
To approve the approach to be
taken to implement the requirements of the Renters Rights Act
2025.
content:
To approve the approach to be
taken to implement the requirements of the Renters Rights Act
2025.

The Cabinet Member amended the existing
Environment & Community Protection Enforcement Policy and
approve updated Housing Enforcement and Civil Penalties Policies
detailed below:

·      
The Housing Enforcement Policy at APPENDIX A and this Policy be
appended to the Enforcement policy in consultation with the Chair
of Regulation and Licensing Committee.

·      
The Civil Penalties Policy at APPENDIX B (penalties will be based
on the calculator provided by Justice for tenants) and that all
income is reinvested in private sector enforcement functions.
 
Noted that the Cabinet Member for Community
and Public Protection in consultation with the Environment and
Community Protection Manager is authorised to make minor changes to
the Civil Penalties and Housing Enforcement Policies.

The Renters Rights Act 2025 obtained Royal
Assent on the 27 October 2025 with reforms being introduced through
a phased approach with a new investigatory power being implemented
from 27 December 2025 and phase 1 commenced on 1 May 2026.
 
 
The Act introduces significant reform of the
private rented sector with the aim of improving security, fairness
and standards for private tenants whilst strengthening enforcement
powers for local authorities.
 
The estimated private rental sector in
Lichfield District is 6,363 using Ministry of Housing, Communities
and Local Government Live Tables on Housing Stock.

The new legislation brings in a duty to
enforce, however the option to issue a civil penalty was introduced
by the Housing and Planning Act in 2016. The Council previously had
a ‘Private Sector Housing Civil Penalties Enforcement
Policy’ as part of the 2020 Enforcement Policy, this was
based on the ‘Nottingham Model’. There was also a
‘Bristol Model’ available at the time. Alternative
civil penalty calculators are therefore available; however, it
became apparent from Housing Tribunals, where Councils lost, that
some areas needed tweaking. Justice for Tenants, who are a non
profit organisation providing free advice, support and training for
Local Authorities and have used specialist legal advisors. Their
model takes account of tribunal results (in effect, case law for
Civil Penalties) and the Renters Rights Act etc. There are
alternatives however there are well over 200 Local Authorities
signed up to Justice for Tenants model and there is safety in their
expertise as well as ongoing feedback from LAs that are using their
model. Whilst the maximum fines are detailed in the legislation, we
are recommending in the Council’s policy an increase in the
early payment discount from 15% to 30%.
topline: The Cabinet Member has decided to approve the implementation of the Renters Rights Act 2025, introducing reforms in the private rented sector.

This report seeks approval to

guidance for applicants, businesses and planning officers,
improving clarity and decision-making.

The Cabinet:
 
2.1 Recommended to Full Council the adoption
of the Lichfield City Centre Shopfront Design Code as a
Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) to support implementation of
existing Local Plan policies.

1. Do Not Adopt
Retain existing policy, resulting in continued inconsistency,
limited improvement, and an inability to prevent design creep.
 
2. Delay Adoption
Postpone adoption, delaying benefits and preventing adoption as an
SPD within the required timeframe.
 
3. Adopt Without SPD Status
Adopt the Design Code as guidance only, limiting its material
weight and effectiveness in decision-making.

This paper provides Cabinet
with an update on the progress the Council has made in developing
its latest Local Plan. In doing so, it reflects on:

·      
the impact the April 2025 update of the National
Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) had on the housing target for
Lichfield district, (increasing it to 746 houses per year - 15,666
over the plan period 2022-2043 - a 158% increase on the previous
target of 289 houses per year), and

·      
the opportunity to develop a deeper evidence base to
support a preferred option for distributing growth across the
district to achieve this revised housing number, provided through
the new Town and Country Planning Regulations under the new
condensed timeframe of 30 months for non ‘legacy
system’ plans

The Cabinet:
 
2.1 Approved a move to a Local Plan submission
under the new 30 month system in line with the Town and Country
Planning Regulations 2026.
 
2.2 Delegated authority to the Cabinet Member
for Housing and the Local Plan in conjunction with the Chief
Executive, to serve the notice of commencement and publish the
timetable for the new Local Plan.

If the proposal to change to the new 30-month
process is approved, it will allow time for the new plan to
adequately address and include options for new settlements - new,
planned communities in appropriate locations, alongside other
approaches. This approach would better ensure that growth can be
planned in the right locations and supported by the necessary
infrastructure, while protecting landscapes, heritage and the
character of the district.
 
While this would extend the overall timeline
for adopting the Local Plan, it would strengthen the
council’s ability to manage development in the long term and
also presents an opportunity to produce a clearer, more
user-friendly plan for the benefit of residents and businesses.

The Council could continue to progress the
Lichfield Local Plan 2043 to submission by December 2026. However,
as the evidence base and the draft final Local Plan is not
complete, this option presents a risk that the timescales for
consultation and the end deadline for submission set by government
cannot be met. There is also the risk that documents produced
within the short timeframe remaining would not meet the
pre-submission requirements or the tests of soundness set out in
the NPPF. If the Local Plan was found unsound during the
examination, the Council could not adopt it
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve a move to a Local Plan submission under the new 30-month system, impacting the housing target for Lichfield district.

day.

enforced, with anyone caught fishing being served a fixed penalty
notice.  It will also enable the
occasional problem with people fishing and causing anti-social
behaviour in the daytime to be dealt with.
 
The proposals have been
considered by the Regulatory and Licensing Committee and
recommended for approval.

content:
To approve for adoption the
Council’s Statement of Licensing Policy 2026 -
2031.

The Council approved the adoption the
statement of licensing policy and cumulative impact assessment.

Under the Licensing Act 2003 the Statement of
Licensing Policy must be reviewed every five years. The Policy has
been updated with the latest legislative changes using the guidance
issued by the Home Office in November 2025.
 
The Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA), which
forms part of the Council’s Statement of Licensing Policy has
been reviewed at the same time. Staffordshire Police has requested
that the cumulative impact assessment area be expanded to cover the
city centre, rather than just Bird Street and Market Street.
 
In addition to the statutory consultees, the
following were also consulted: Responsible Authorities, District
Councillors, District & County Council groups including
Community Safety, Health & Safety, Environmental Protection,
Trading Standards, Highways, District Councillors, Responsible
Bodies Group, Town Centres Manager, Licensing solicitors and agents
and breweries.
 
This policy was presented to and approved by
the Regulatory and Licensing Committee, prior to a 4 week consultation. It was subsequently taken back
to the Regulatory and Licensing Committee following concerns around
the CIA extension proposals.
 
At the meeting on 26 February 2026, the

content:
To deliver a high-quality
regeneration scheme for Lichfield City Centre by recovering,
renovating or replacing selected shop fronts. The city centre
businesses will be guided by a detailed design code that aids
owners create and sustain high quality, attractive frontages in
line with the city’s traditional streetscape.

The Cabinet:
 
2.1 Approves the development of a Heritage
Shop Front Design Code for Lichfield City Centre.
 
2.2 Approves the introduction of a grant
scheme to support the Lichfield City Centre Heritage Shop Frontage
Scheme.
 
2.3 Cabinet delegates authority to the Cabinet
Member to approve the finalised Shopfront Improvement Grant Scheme,
including scoring criteria, triage pathways, grant agreements,
monitoring requirements, and payment structure.
 
2.4 Approved development of a Heritage Lottery
Fund grant application, seeking external funding to further support
the implementation of the Shop Front Design Code across the city
centre.

The Shop Frontage Heritage Grant Scheme will
support the implementation of the emerging Design Code, ensuring
consistency, quality, and character-led improvements across the
area. Providing financial support to incentivise participation and
reduce the cost burden on small businesses.
 
The grant scheme will encourage property
owners and tenants to restore shop frontages to their authentic
early period heritage appearance enhancing the visual quality,
historic character, and economic vitality of the town centre.
 
This strengthened framework will align fully
with the Council’s conservation approach and, while grant
funding will not be used for enforcement, the adoption of a clear,
city centre specific design code will better support planning
enforcement activity where required to act against unauthorised or
poor quality alterations helping to
safeguard the long-term integrity of the conservation area

1. Do Nothing – Without an adopted Shop
Frontage Heritage Grant Scheme the shop owners will face financial
burden to ensure their properties are in line with the current and
emerging extensive design code update.
 
2. Restart the process – Pursuing a
different grant scheme is unlikely to produce any new options. This
approach would leave the City Centre in its current condition, with
a great risk of further decline.
 
3. Proceed without an enhanced City Centre
Design Code - Launch the grant scheme using existing policy and
guidance. This approach can still target key streets and deliver
improvements, but overall coherence across shopfronts is likely to
be more limited and less impactful.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to implement a Heritage Shop Front Design Code and grant scheme to support the regeneration of Lichfield City Centre.

content:
The Cabinet Member approved to direct award
the contract for the refurbishment of the wet-side changing area at
Burntwood Leisure Centre to Ascot Services, in line with the
Councils Contract Procedure Riles via the Procure Partnership
Framework, within the agreed budget.

The refurbishment of the wet side changing
area at Burntwood Leisure Centre is essential to maintain the
Council’s asset, improving user experience, and preventing
further deterioration that could lead to increased future repair
costs.
 
A compliant and transparent market engagement
exercise was undertaken via Procure Partnership Framework. Six
potential contractors were initially identified, a contractor was
initially engaged first based on their experience with similar
works. Following detailed cost review, the contractors pricing did
not align with the approved project budget. As a result, the
Council revisited the framework to identify alternative contractors
able to deliver the project within the budget and timescales.
 
Following the reassessment of suitable
framework contractors, Ascot Services were identified as a
compliant contractor eligible for direct award under the
framework.
 
•          
Ascot provided baseline costs that are fully aligned with the
approved budget
•          
Their proposal demonstrates capacity, experience, and value for
money
•          
This makes Ascot the most economically advantageous and deliverable
option within the required timeframe
 
Ascot Services have already undertaken a
baseline costing exercise for the project and have confirmed:
 
•          
Material supply chains in place
•          
Ability to procure at competitive framework rates
•          
Availability to meet the required delivery window
This enables the Council to mobilise works
quickly without further delay.
 
 
Awarding the contract directly to Ascot
Services mitigates the risks associated with:
 
•          
Re-tendering
•          
Extending the programme
•          
Further price inflation
•          
Disruption to centre users
Proceeding via direct award ensures the
project remains within budget and can be delivered at pace.
 
Ascot’s baseline costs provide:
 
•          
Budget certainty
•          
Reduced mobilisation risk
•          
Delivery within the agreed financial envelope
Their framework rates and immediate
availability offer a cost-efficient and timely solution for the
Council.

Re-running the procurement process would delay
the project and risk missing the critical completion deadlines.
topline: The Cabinet Member has decided to award the contract for the refurbishment of Burntwood Leisure Centre to Ascot Services.

content:
The purpose of this report is
to update Cabinet on the recent strategic Community Infrastructure
Levy (CIL) application process and seek approval to allocate
£1,475,534 of strategic CIL funding to twelve applicants. It
outlines the evaluation process undertaken by the Strategic
Infrastructure Group (SIG) for applications received in December
2025.
 
The next strategic CIL funding
round will open in Spring 2026

CIL enables local planning authorities to
raise funds from developers undertaking new building projects in
their area. The money can be used to fund a wide range of
infrastructure that is needed to support the development of the
area.
 
The CIL Regulations 2010 specify that CIL
income must be allocated as follows:

•      
Administration Fund: up to 5% of CIL income can be used for
implementing and administering CIL by the charging authority.

•      
Neighbourhood Fund: 15% (subject to a cap based on the number of
existing dwellings in the parish) rising to 25% in areas with a
Neighbourhood Plan, is passed to the Parish Council where the
contributing development is located.

•      
Strategic Infrastructure: The remaining 70-80% must be spent on
infrastructure that supports growth within the CIL Charging
Authority’s area.
 
This report only covers the allocation of
strategic CIL funding and not the allocations to Parish Councils.
Neighbourhood CIL (NCIL) funding is spent at the discretion of the
individual parish councils and must be spent within 5 years of
receipt. Parish Councils are required to report annually on their
NCIL spending and these reports can be viewed online.

Cabinet could decide to not allocate any
funding to any of the projects and continue to accrue monies to
create a larger pot that can be used for delivery of some of the
projects that were not successful in this round or new projects in
a further bidding round. This approach would contradict the
council’s own adopted procedures which state that the Council
will open a CIL bidding round each year in line with its adopted
Infrastructure List. It also risks CIL funding being applied to
lower scoring projects that do not align with the Council’s
infrastructure priorities.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to allocate £1,475,534 of strategic Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) funding to twelve applicants.

The Cabinet Member approved the award of the
contract for the Fradley Play Park improvement project to Creative
Play Ltd, identified as the highest-scoring and most advantageous
tenderer following evaluation.

Cabinet member approval was granted in
November 2025 for the application of £193,500 of Section 106
financial contributions, towards improvements to the Worthington
Road and Barlow Drive play areas, both Fradley Parish Council
assets. Fradley Parish Council have agreed to fund an additional
£84,303.90 totalling the project value to
£277,803.90.
 
A full design brief and specification were
developed based on site assessments and consultation with Fradley
Parish Council and local ward members. The specification included
requirements for improved play value, inclusive equipment, safety
surfacing, and durability to support long-term use by the
community.
 
A compliant tendering process has been carried
out with the support of the council's procurement
service. 

1. Refurbish existing equipment only –
this would not deliver uplift required and would not provide
long-term resilience of the facilities
 
2. Refurbish only one site – A suitable
solution has been found within budget to refurbish both sites.
 
3. Do nothing – The existing equipment
is outdated and does not meet current safety and accessibility
standards.
 
4. Re-tender – A suitable solution has
been found so this wouldn’t be a good use of officer
time.
topline: The Cabinet Member has decided to award a contract for improvements to play areas in Fradley Parish.

purpose:
Under Part 2 and Schedule 1 of
the Housing (Right to Enfranchise) (Designated Protected Areas)
(England) Order 2009, certain parishes of the district are classed
as Designated Protected Areas (DPA). The designation of a DPA
impacts the lease agreement of shared ownership properties as it
would either restrict staircasing to 80% of the overall property
value, or if the lease allows staircasing to exceed 80%, it places
an obligation on the leaseholder to sell their property back to
their RP landlord. 
 
As DPA rules make it more
difficult to sell shared ownership homes and can reduce their
financial viability, Homes England recognises that these
restrictions are not always necessary.   Therefore, if a local authority or
registered provider can show that retaining shared ownership stock
is not a local concern, Homes England is willing to consider
requests to waive the usual DPA conditions attached to grant
funding.
 
This report outlines the
negative impact of the DPA on the RP and prospective shared
ownership owners and recommends that we submit an application to
Home England to waive the conditions that apply to land within the
DPA of The Lakes development, Curborough 22/00040/REMM Land North
East of Watery Lane, Curborough, Lichfield.

purpose:
The decision is to determine
whether Lichfield District Council should agree to enter into a
Section 106 agreement to monitor the proposed Grove Farm Habitat
Bank for a period of 30 years.
content:
The decision is to determine
whether Lichfield District Council should agree to enter into a
Section 106 agreement to monitor the proposed Grove Farm Habitat
Bank for a period of 30 years.

To approve to enter into the S106 agreement at
Appendix 1 for Grove Farm Habitat Bank at Grove Farm, Burton Road,
Whittington, Lichfield WS13 8QN that will include a 30 year Habitat
Management and Monitoring Plan.

The Environment Act 2021 required all
development in England to provide a minimum of 10% biodiversity net
gain. Where this gain cannot be delivered on site, developers must
seek to offset this requirement off site, either through the
purchase of BUs from a registered Habitat Bank, or by purchasing
Biodiversity Credits from Natural England.
 
The Act also put a Duty on us as a Local
Planning Authority to ensure that sufficient BUs are available for
offsetting in our district (more easily allowing development to
fulfil the statutory requirement).
 
By agreeing to enter into a 30-year agreement
to monitor the delivery and condition of the proposed Grove Farm
Habitat Bank, it will allow the Bank to be listed on the Natural
England Biodiversity Gain Sites Register and begin to officially
operate as a Habitat Bank (that is, to provide Biodiversity Units
to developers to meet their Statutory Biodiversity Net Gain
requirement). This will enable more development to take place in
the district, by providing local (and therefore more
cost-effective) Biodiversity Units for local developments.
 
The site (approx. 26ha) is currently in arable
use and is intensively managed. It is proposed to enhance the site
to provide approximately 12ha of mixed scrub and 14ha of
traditional orchard – resulting in 131.74 BUs being created.
By bringing the land out of arable use and into active management
for biodiversity benefit, the site will positively contribute to
both Lichfield District and UK national biodiversity goals.


1.    
For amendments to be made to the S106 & HMMP. These will then
need to be conveyed and agreed by all parties before signing and
sealing can take place. 
 

2.    
For Lichfield District Council to not enter into this
agreement.
topline: The Cabinet Member Decision has decided to approve entering into a 30-year agreement to monitor the Grove Farm Habitat Bank for biodiversity net gain.

content:
To approve the freehold
acquisition of a two bed house in Lichfield for the sale price of
£265,000, with a further £6,000 set aside for
associated legal costs and repair/maintenance works.

The Leader approved the freehold acquisition
of a two bed house in Lichfield for the sale price of
£265,000, with a further £6,000 set aside for
associated legal costs and repair/maintenance works.
 
The Leader noted that this purchase will see
the total number of properties purchased with the £2m to two,
leaving approximately six further purchases to be made.
 
The Leader noted that the council will work
with Homes England ongoing to determine whether any external
funding is available to contribute to the purchase and delivery of
this accommodation unit. Should funding be available, any
underspend of capital monies to fund this property will be
maintained in the capital budget for further purchases.

There is a limited supply of temporary
accommodation and social rented housing units in the district. As a
result, oftentimes families and individuals are placed in bed and
breakfast accommodation with limited facilities outside of the
bedroom, making it unsuitable for long-term placements.
 
Last year, the council spent approximately
£191,000 on temporary accommodation (the exact amount of this
may differ) Delivering approximately eight new units of temporary
accommodation will help to provide more suitable homes to local
people facing housing crisis, ensure that rent paid is reinvested
into quality temporary accommodation and reduce the council’s
overall spend 
 
The team’s work will be focused on
purchasing and refurbishing existing properties, which the council
has identified is the swiftest and most efficient way to deliver
much-needed homes in the locations where people need them most.
This will ensure a swift turnaround of properties and maximise our
ability to provide immediate assistance to those in need.
 
The council’s wholly owned trading
company, Lichfield West Midlands Traded Services (LWMTS), will also
provide property management support and the tenants will be
supported by our housing team.
 
The council will be purchasing properties in
key locations, including Lichfield City, Burntwood, Fazeley and
Armitage with Handsacre, to provide
residents with easy access to shops, transport, and local
services
 
When choosing properties, the team focuses on
properties that are near to:
•               
Public transport.
•               
Supermarkets offering good value products.
•               
Schools.
•               
Health centres.
•               
Community facilities
 
Research with individuals who need to move
into temporary accommodation has indicated they need easy access to
all of the above. An equalities impact assessment has been carried
out on our approach to property selection and purchase.

There were no other alternative options
given.
topline: The Leader of the Council has decided to approve the acquisition of a two bed house in Lichfield to provide more suitable homes for local residents in need.

purpose:
The council processes council
tax payments, benefits payments, and sundry debt administration
through a revenues and benefits system, which customers interact
with on a daily basis, both online, through customer services and
through our revenues and benefits team.
 
In September the council
approved the procurement of the NEC revenues and benefits
back-office system for five years, with the option to extend for a
further two years, on the basis it has been assessed as the most
cost-effective and operationally sound option.
 
It delegated the selection of
the customer front-end system (either enhancing NEC or
transitioning to a comparable front-end solution) to the
responsible director, cabinet member, and s151 officer, subject to
usability testing, procurement processes and costs being within
Approved Budgets.
 
Analysis of available options
has been carried out and it has been determined that remaining with
NEC for the front-end solution is the recommended solution on the
basis that it delivers improved usability and accessibility, avoids
significant disruption and customer confusion, minimises
operational and financial risk, and prevents the need for major
system change during a critical period leading up to LGR and annual
billing. Accordingly, this paper recommends procuring the NEC
system customer front-end system together with the NEC back-office
system, as a single procurement.
 
The procurement will be made
through a procurement compliant direct award on the VAS Framework.
With the advent of local government reorganisation, the VAS
Framework also includes a 90-day termination clause that will
enable the council or any future council to move away from the
contract with minimal financial impact should a change of system be
required by the future unitary council.

purpose:

acquisition of a three-bed house in Burntwood for the sale price of
£260,000, with a further £6,000 set aside for
associated legal costs and repair/maintenance works.
content:
To approve the freehold
acquisition of a three-bed house in Burntwood for the sale price of
£260,000, with a further £6,000 set aside for
associated legal costs and repair/maintenance works.

The Leader approves the freehold acquisition
of a three-bed house in Burntwood for the sale price of
£260,000, with a further £6,000 set aside for
associated legal costs and repair/maintenance works.
 
The Leader notes that this purchase will see
the total number of properties purchased with the £2m to one,
leaving approximately seven further purchases to be made.
 
The Leader notes that the council will work
with Homes England ongoing to determine whether any external
funding is available to contribute to the purchase and delivery of
this accommodation unit. Should funding be available, any
underspend of capital monies to fund this property will be
maintained in the capital budget for further purchases.

There is a limited supply of temporary
accommodation and social rented housing units in the district. As a
result, oftentimes families and individuals are placed in bed and
breakfast accommodation with limited facilities outside of the
bedroom, making it unsuitable for long-term placements. 
 
Last year, the council spent approximately
£191,000 on temporary accommodation ( the exact amount of
this may differ ) Delivering approximately eight new units of
temporary accommodation will help to provide more suitable homes to
local people facing housing crisis, ensure that rent paid is
reinvested into quality temporary accommodation and reduce the
council’s overall spend 
 
The team’s work will be focused on
purchasing and refurbishing existing properties, which the council
has identified is the swiftest and most efficient way to deliver
much-needed homes in the locations where people need them most.
This will ensure a swift turnaround of properties and maximise our
ability to provide immediate assistance to those in need.
 
The council’s wholly owned trading
company, Lichfield West Midlands Traded Services (LWMTS), will also
provide property management support and the tenants will be
supported by our housing team.
 
The council will be purchasing properties in
key locations, including Lichfield City, Burntwood, Fazeley and
Armitage with Handsacre, to provide
residents with easy access to shops, transport, and local
services
 
When choosing properties, the team focuses on
properties that are near to:

·      
Public transport.

·      
Supermarkets offering good value products.

·      
Schools.

·      
Health centres.

·      
Community facilities
 
Research with individuals who need to move
into temporary accommodation has         
indicated they need easy access to all of the above. An equalities
impact assessment has been carried out on our approach to property
selection and purchase.

There were no other alternative options
given.
topline: The Leader of the Council has decided to approve the acquisition of a three-bed house in Burntwood for £260,000 to address the shortage of temporary accommodation and social rented housing units in the district.

purpose:
Approval is sought for the
allocation of £193,500 of financial contributions in the
Section 106 Agreement ‘Land at Fradley Park, Halifax
Avenue’ towards improvements to play areas within Fradley

content:
Approval is sought for the
allocation of £193,500 of financial contributions in the
Section 106 Agreement ‘Land at Fradley Park, Halifax
Avenue’ towards improvements to play areas within Fradley
Parish.
 
 

To allocate £193,500 of the
‘Social and Community Sum’ financial contributions in
the Section 106 Agreement for ‘Land at Fradley Park, Halifax
Avenue’, planning application 10/01498/OUT, towards the
following project within Fradley Parish: Play area improvements
within Fradley village.

The Section 106 Agreement for ‘Land at
Fradley Park, Halifax Avenue’ (planning application
10/01498/OUT), signed on 24th October 2013, secured financial
contributions collectively known as the ‘Social and Community
Sum’. The value of these contributions is £193,500. In
terms of the contributions’ legal purpose, the Agreement
states the following:‘…to
be used by the District Council for the provision or maintenance of
health facilities public art and social facilities (to include
changing facilities linked to off-site pitch provision).’
 
The Parish Council are working with Lichfield
West Midlands Trading Services (LWMTS) to deliver improvements to
two play areas within Fradley village and the total budget for the
project is £277,803.  The project
satisfies the Social and Community Sum’s legal purpose by
improving and maintaining social facilities within Fradley
parish, therefore it is recommended that
the £193,500 contribution is allocated towards this
project.


The alternative options were considered:





 Option?



Consideration?



Selected
option?





Not to allocate the Section
106 financial contribution towards the play area improvements
within Fradley and instead allocate
towards an alternative project.



This option is not recommended as the project meets
the S106 requirements and the financial contributions are required
to be allocated by a specific date (in this case February 2026)
otherwise it risks being claimed back by the developer. The Council
should also be proactive in allocating S106 contributions towards
projects which satisfy the specific requirements as set out within
the Agreement.



Allocate the S106
contribution towards the play area improvements
topline: The Cabinet Member Decision has decided to allocate £193,500 towards play area improvements in Fradley Parish.

content:
Cabinet agreed:
 
To approve the publication of the IFS
(Appendix A) on the website, in line with statutory requirements
set out in the Community Infrastructure Levy (Amendment) (England)
(No. 2) Regulations 2019.
 
To note the monies received, held and spent
from CIL and s106 in the financial year 2024/2025.
 
To approve the proposed Infrastructure List
(IL), which outlines a shortlist of strategic projects and/or types
of projects eligible for CIL funding applications in 2025/2026

This report presents the 2025 annual
Infrastructure Funding Statement (IFS) and revised Infrastructure
List (IL). It details the amount of Community Infrastructure Levy
(CIL) and Section 106 (S106) monies received and spent during the
2024/25 financial year.
 
The IL outlines the strategic infrastructure
projects that the council considers eligible for CIL funding
applications this financial year. It reflects priorities identified
in the Infrastructure Delivery Plan (IDP), adopted Local Plan,
Lichfield District 2050 Strategy and ongoing discussions with
infrastructure providers.

IFS Financial Report:
• No other options have been considered
as the IFS is a factual record
setting out developer contributions received
and how they have been
used. It is a legal requirement to publish an
IFS no later than 31st
December each year. The content is dictated by
the Community
Infrastructure Levy (Amendment) (England) (No.
2) Regulations 2019.
Infrastructure List:
• The council could choose to not adopt
the proposed Infrastructure List and
revert to the previous process of open
bidding. This may result in a larger
number of projects bidding for CIL monies and
risks CIL being awarded to
projects that do not support the Local Plan
but score highly using the
previous criteria. This approach would
contradict the council’s own
adopted procedures and the requirements set
out in the Community
Infrastructure Regulations. As such, a new
approach would need to be
established to ensure the council undertakes
its duties in respect of
planning obligations.
• The council could establish an
alternative approach to the governance and
administration of CIL monies to that proposed.
The council can adopt any
approach it sees fit, however the one proposed
has regard to best practice
from other authorities and was approved by
Cabinet on 5th March 2024.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Infrastructure Funding Statement and Infrastructure List for the financial year 2024/2025, outlining strategic projects eligible for Community Infrastructure Levy funding applications.

purpose:
To consider the Council’s
Local Government Reorganisation proposal.
content:
To consider the Council’s
Local Government Reorganisation proposal.

Council recommended:
 
That Cabinet approves the preferred option, a
three unitary model to cover Staffordshire and Stokeon-Trent, as
set out in the full submission document at Appendix 1.
 
That Cabinet delegates finalising the full
submission document to the Leader of the Council, in consultation
with the Chief Executive, prior to submitting to Government by the
28 November 2025 deadline.

In December 2024, the Government published a
White Paper (Power and Partnership: Foundations for Growth) setting
out their plans for devolution and Local Government Reorganisation
(‘the White Paper’) alongside the process for
determining the future structure of local government in two tier
areas, and their timetable for its implementation.
 
The reasons Government gave for a need for
Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) in areas like Staffordshire
are rooted in both efficiency goals and its broader devolution
ambitions:
• Government is seeking to create
simpler, clearer local government structures that are easier for
residents to understand and navigate.
• Their view is clearly that the current
two-tier system leads to confusion and duplication of services.
• Equally, reorganisation is expected to
unlock efficiency savings by reducing administrative overheads and
streamlining service delivery.
• It is also believed that a single-tier
system will enhance local democratic accountability, with clearer
lines of responsibility for services.
• LGR aligns with the goals of the
Government’s English Devolution White Paper and the
Devolution Priority Programme.
• Then, larger unitary authorities are
expected to provide stronger regional leadership, better strategic
planning, and more effective use of resources.
 
Local authorities in two-tier areas were
invited to submit initial proposals for Local Government
Reorganisation by 21 March 2025, with final proposals to be
submitted in November.
 
Lichfield District Council worked with
neighbouring authorities (Cannock Chase, South Staffordshire,
Stafford, Tamworth and East Staffordshire) in the development of an
interim plan, which Council endorsed at its meeting on 18 March
2025.
 
Following the submission of the Interim Plan,
the Council continued to work with neighbouring authorities on
developing a detailed evidence base and investigating our options
for LGR. This has led to a preferred option being identified and
this paper introduces it, our final proposal, for Council’s
endorsement before Cabinet meets to formally determine the best
option for the residents of our district.
 
Final proposals must be submitted to
Government by 28 November 2025.

Do nothing - The Secretary of State retains
the power to implement reorganisation even if councils do not
submit proposals.
 
Support another option – The three
unitary proposal, with two unitaries covering
the south of the county, is the only option
that will preserve the “local touch” that
people value: services designed around local
needs, councillors who listen, and
greater accountability. This option also
provides clear opportunities for saving
money, removing duplication, simplifying
services, and maintaining the character
and traditions of our communities
topline: The Council has decided to approve a three unitary model for Local Government Reorganisation in Staffordshire and Stokeon-Trent.
